tracks.title: Little Moons (ages 6–8)
tracks.blurb: Money, earning, saving, spending, companies and staying safe. Lots of pictures and sorting.

tracks.title: Big Moons (ages 9–11)
tracks.blurb: Shares, borrowing, prices over time, report cards, charts and why prices move. Clues, never promises.

tracks.title: Full Moons (challenge)
tracks.blurb: Extra challenge for any age: percents, fees, borrowing math and the Rule of 72. Always optional. Still clues, never promises.

objectives.text: Explain why people use money instead of trading things.
Say that most people earn money by working.
Sort needs from wants.
Describe a budget as a plan made before spending.
Name what you give up when you choose (a trade-off).
Describe a company as a team that sells goods or services.
Work out profit as money in minus money out.
Explain that companies can sell shares to raise money to grow.
Explain that a share is a small piece of a company.
Describe what being a part owner means, including that value can rise or fall.
Say where shares are traded.
Explain that prices move when buyers or sellers are more eager.
Recognize a ticker as a company's short name on the market.
Tell saving (stays the same) from investing (can grow or shrink).
Describe interest as extra money a bank pays.
Explain why starting early helps growth pile up.
Sort choices by low and high risk.
Choose saving for soon and investing for a long time away.
Explain a dividend as profit shared with owners.
Explain why some companies keep profit to grow.
Compare spending a dividend with reinvesting it.
Explain why the price can drop by about the dividend on its cut-off day.
Explain why spreading money across many companies lowers the risk from any one company.
Explain why long-term investors don't react to one bad day.
Tell hype from facts and ask who is talking and why.
Spot a too-good-to-be-true promise and ask a grown-up.
Describe a company report card (earnings report) and how often it comes.
Explain that experts estimate profit per share before the report.
Decide beat or miss by comparing the result with the estimate.
Explain why a price can fall on a beat (expectations).
Explain guidance as a company's own guess about what comes next.
Explain why prices move fast on report day.
Say that Piggy Bank coins are pretend and follow real prices.
Work out how spreading coins limits the hurt from one company.
Explain why time can smooth out ups and downs, without a promise.
Treat a down day as normal, not a mistake.
Choose to check now and then instead of every minute.
Use the whole market's move as a clue.
Use a group's (sector's) move as a clue.
Compare a move with its normal size.
Say "we're not sure" when there are no clues.
Read a candle's body and color.
Read a candle's high and low from its wicks.
Recognize a tug-of-war day (small body, long wicks).
Tell an up trend from a down trend.
Recognize a sideways trend, and that trends can change.
Zoom out instead of judging by one day.
Find a floor (support) and a ceiling (resistance), and that they can break.
Recognize a breakout and that many fail.
Explain why chart shapes look obvious only after the fact.
Treat chart shapes as clues, never promises.
Explain volume as how many shares were traded.
Explain a moving average as a smooth, backward-looking line.
Explain why report day can bring big moves either way.
List jobs and the skills they need, and how new skills can raise pay.
Tell wages, salaries and tips apart, and work out pay for hours worked.
Explain that an entrepreneur starts a business, takes a risk, and earns a profit only if money in is more than money out.
Explain that taxes come out of income and pay for things a community shares.
Name gifts and allowance as income that may need no work, and plan it too.
Make a savings plan: a goal, an amount each week, and how many weeks.
Use simple tricks to wait for something better later (delay gratification).
Explain why saving is often harder than spending, and how ads push spending now.
Explain an emergency (rainy day) fund.
Compare keeping savings at home with a bank or credit union (safe, tracked, may pay interest).
Compare prices for the same thing before buying.
Spot how ads and friends push us to buy, and find reliable facts.
Tell cash, debit cards and credit cards apart.
Know that game coins and gems are often bought with real money, and ask a grown-up first.
Describe giving money, things or time to help others.
Explain that borrowed money or things must be paid back.
Explain interest as the price of borrowing, so a borrower pays back more.
Explain why lenders lend (they earn interest) and why paying back on time builds trust.
Explain that a credit card is a loan, and when it usually costs no interest.
Show how unpaid debt grows with interest on interest.
Define inflation as most prices going up over time.
Explain that money kept the same buys less when prices rise.
Compare a savings rate with rising prices.
Describe a fund as a basket holding many companies.
Explain an index fund as buying every company on a list, often with low fees.
Show how a yearly fee lowers what you end up with.
Explain spreading across groups, since companies in one group often move together.
Give examples of risk and ways to make it smaller.
Explain insurance as many people paying a little so one person isn't hurt a lot.
Keep passwords, codes and addresses private.
Spot scam red flags (rushing, secrets, prizes you pay for) and tell a grown-up.
Compare growth on growth (compound) with the same extra each year (simple).
Use the Rule of 72 to guess how long growth takes to double.
Explain that report dates are set ahead, and when the price can react (before the open or after the close).
Work out profit for each share (earnings per share).
Tell sales (revenue) from profit, and why more sales can still mean less profit.
Judge the size of a beat or miss compared with the guess.
Compare dividends as dollars paid for each $100 of share price, and know they can be cut.

units.title: Money basics
units.blurb: What money is, and how to plan it.
talk: What did you buy last? Was it a need or a want?
If you had $5, what would you give up to get the thing you picked?
Let's set up three jars at home: Spend, Save and Give. How much goes in each?

steps.text: Long ago, people traded things. A cow for some bread!
That was hard. What if the baker did not want a cow?
So people made money. Everyone agrees it is worth something, so everyone takes it.

steps.q: Why did people start using money?
steps.why: Money makes trading easy, because everyone takes it.

steps.text: Grown-ups earn money by doing work. A cook cooks. A nurse helps sick people.
With a grown-up's OK, kids can earn too. You can sell lemonade or help a neighbor.
A bank machine does not make money. It gives back money that was put in first.

steps.q: How do most grown-ups get money?
options: The bank gives it out for free
The store gives it to them
steps.why: Most grown-ups earn money by doing a job.

steps.text: A need is something you must have. Like food, a home and clothes.
A want is something nice to have. Like a new game or candy.

steps.q: Is it a need or a want?
steps.why: Needs come first. Wants come next, if there is money left.

steps.text: A budget is a plan for your money. You plan before you spend.
Try three jars: Spend, Save and Give. Put some money in each one.
When you see something fun, check your Spend jar first.

steps.q: A budget is…
steps.why: A budget is a plan. It helps you choose before you spend.

steps.text: You have $5. You can get a kite or a book. Not both!
When you pick one thing, you give up the other one. That is called a trade-off.
Good choosers ask: What do I give up if I pick this?

steps.q: Sam has $5. He picks candy instead of a kite. What did Sam give up?
steps.why: Sam picked candy, so he gave up the kite. The kite is the trade-off.

units.title: Earning money
units.blurb: Jobs, skills, getting paid and taxes.
talk: What jobs do grown-ups in our family do? What skills does each job need, and how did they learn them?
If you started a small business, what would you sell? What would you need to buy first?
On the way to school, find one thing taxes paid for. Who uses it?

steps.text: People do lots of jobs. A cook makes food. A vet helps pets. A builder makes homes.
Each job needs skills. People get skills by learning and lots of practice.
Jobs that need more training often pay more. Every job helps someone.

steps.q: How can people earn more over time?
options: Wait for the bank to pay them
steps.why: New skills and practice can help people earn more.

steps.text: Sometimes money comes as a gift, like a birthday card from Grandma.
Some kids get an allowance. That is money from family, often each week.
Gift or allowance, it helps to make a plan before you spend it.

steps.q: Your aunt gives you $10 for your birthday. What is it?
steps.why: A gift is money you get without doing a job, and you keep it.

steps.text: Someone who starts a business is called an entrepreneur. A lemonade stand counts!
First you pay for things like lemons and cups. Then you hope people buy.
You spend $6 on lemons and cups. You sell 10 cups for $1 each.
It is a risk. If not enough people buy, you can lose money.

steps.q: Why is starting a business a risk?
options: You have to be a grown-up
A business never pays for things
steps.why: You pay first and hope people buy. If they don't, you can lose money.

steps.text: Some workers get paid for each hour they work. That pay is called a wage.
Some get the same pay each year, split into paychecks. That is a salary.
Some also get tips. A tip is extra money a customer gives for good help.
Ana helps at a bake sale for $5 an hour. She works 3 hours and gets a $2 tip.

steps.q: Leo earns $10 an hour. He works 3 hours. What does he earn?
steps.why: 3 hours × $10 an hour is $30.

lessons.title: Taxes pay for what we share

steps.text: Part of the money people earn goes to the government. That part is called taxes.
Some things we buy have a little tax added too.
Taxes help pay for things we all share. Schools, roads, parks and fire trucks.

steps.q: Paid by taxes, or by one family?
steps.why: Taxes pay for things a whole town shares. Families pay for their own things.

steps.q: Ben earns $100. $10 goes to taxes. What does he take home?
steps.why: $100 take away $10 of taxes is $90.

units.title: Saving goals
units.blurb: Plan ahead, wait for it, and keep it safe.
talk: What is one thing you'd like to save up for? Let's work out how many weeks it would take.
Tell about a time you waited for something. Was it worth the wait? What helped you wait?
Do people in our family feel the same way about saving? Why might people feel differently? Where do we keep our savings?

steps.text: A saving goal is something you save up for. Like a new bike!
A savings plan says how much you will save, and how often.
The bike costs $60. You save $10 each week.

steps.q: Mia saves $2 a week for a $10 game. How many weeks?
steps.why: $2 a week for 5 weeks is $10.

steps.text: Would you take one treat now, or two treats if you wait a bit?
Waiting is hard! Saving means waiting now, so you can get something you want more later.
Tricks help. Put the money out of sight. Draw your goal. Count how close you are.

steps.q: Helps you wait, or makes it harder?

items.text: Money in a jar on a high shelf
Lots of ads for new toys

steps.why: Hiding the money and picturing your goal help. Ads and toy aisles make waiting harder.

steps.text: You can keep savings in a jar at home. But jars can get lost or spent.
A bank keeps money safe. It keeps track of every dollar.
In the US, the government protects savings at most banks, up to a big limit.
Many banks pay a little extra, called interest. They lend savings to others, who pay the bank interest.

steps.q: Why might a bank be better than a jar at home?
steps.why: A bank keeps money safe, keeps track of it, and may pay a little interest.

steps.text: Spending feels good right now. Saving feels good later. That is why saving is hard.
Ads are made to make you want things right now.
Before you spend, ask: Do I want this more than my goal?

steps.q: Why is saving often harder than spending?
options: The fun of spending comes right away
steps.why: Spending is fun now. The prize for saving comes later.

steps.text: Surprises can cost money. A bike tire pops. A window cracks.
Money saved just for surprises is an emergency fund. Some call it a rainy day fund.
With money set aside, a surprise is a bump, not a big problem.

steps.q: What is an emergency fund for?
steps.why: It is money kept ready for surprises, like a fix or a repair.

units.title: Smart spending
units.blurb: Compare, spot ads, pay wisely and give.
talk: Next time we shop, compare two prices together. Which is the better deal, and why?
What ad did you see lately? What did it want you to feel? What did it leave out?
Look at a receipt together. Was it paid with cash, debit or credit? Who would you like to help this month?

steps.text: The same thing can cost different amounts in different stores.
Smart shoppers compare. They look at the price before they pick.
The same teddy bear is in two stores.

steps.q: The same ball costs $7 at one store and $4 at another. Which costs less?
steps.why: $4 is less than $7, so that store costs less.

steps.text: Some games sell gems or coins. They look like pretend money.
But they are often paid for with real money, from a grown-up's card.
Always ask a grown-up before you pay for anything in a game. Small buys add up.

steps.q: A game says "500 gems for $5!" What do you do?
options: Tap it fast before it's gone
steps.why: Gems can cost real money. Always ask a grown-up first.

steps.text: Giving means using money, things or time to help others.
Your Give jar can help a friend, a food bank or an animal shelter.
You can give time too. Like walking dogs at a shelter.

steps.q: Giving money, or giving time?
steps.why: You can help with money from your Give jar, or with your time.

steps.text: Borrowing means using something now and giving it back later.
You borrow a library book. You bring it back by the due date.
Borrowed money works the same way. You must pay it back, even after it is spent.

steps.q: Sam borrows $5 from his sister. What must he do?
options: Keep it, it is his now
Ask the bank to pay her
steps.why: Borrowed money must be paid back, even if it is already spent.

steps.text: A company makes an ad to get you to buy. Ads show the best parts only.
Friends can make us want things too. That push is called peer pressure.
To learn the facts, check with a grown-up. Look at the price and what it really does.

steps.q: Ad trick or a fact you can check?
steps.why: Tricks rush you or make you feel left out. Facts are things you can check.

steps.text: Cash is paper money and coins. When it is spent, it is gone.
A debit card takes money from your own bank account right away.
A credit card borrows the money. You must pay it back later, sometimes with extra.

steps.q: Your own money, or borrowed?
steps.why: Cash and debit use your own money. Credit and loans are borrowed and must be paid back.

units.title: Staying safe with money
units.blurb: Risk, insurance, private info and scams.
talk: What is our family's rule for passwords and codes? Let's agree on one together.
Make up a pretend scam message. Can you spot every red flag in it?
What things do grown-ups buy insurance for, like a car or a home? What does it protect?

steps.text: Risk is a chance that things don't go the way you hope. Like falling off a bike.
We can make risk smaller. A helmet doesn't stop falls, but it helps keep you safe.

steps.q: Makes the risk smaller, or bigger?
steps.why: Helmets and locks make risk smaller. Rushing and carrying everything make it bigger.

steps.text: Some things are private. Your password, your home address, and codes sent to a grown-up's phone.
Tricksters may pretend to be a friend or a game helper to get them.
Never share private things online. If someone asks, tell a grown-up.

steps.q: Okay to share, or keep private?
steps.why: Fun facts are fine. Passwords and addresses stay private.

steps.text: A message says, "Free gems! Just type your password."
That is a scam. A scam is a trick to take your money or your account.
Real games never ask for your password in a chat. Close it and tell a grown-up.

steps.q: Someone online offers free coins for your password. What do you do?
options: Say no and tell a grown-up
steps.why: Nobody needs your password. Free prizes for it are a trick.

steps.text: Scams often have red flags. They rush you. They ask you to keep a secret.
They promise a big prize, but first you must pay or share something private.

steps.q: Red flag, or no red flag?
steps.why: Rushing, secrets and paying for a prize are red flags. When unsure, ask a grown-up.

steps.text: A cracked phone or a dented car can cost a lot to fix. That is a risk.
With insurance, many people each pay a small amount. That amount is called a premium.
When something bad happens to one of them, the insurance company helps pay.

steps.q: How does insurance help?
options: Many pay a little, so one won't pay a lot
It is free money for everyone
steps.why: Everyone pays a little, so the few with bad luck get help.

units.title: Companies
units.blurb: Who makes the things you love.
talk: Find three things at home and name the company that made each one.
If you ran a lemonade stand, what would your money out be?

steps.text: A company is a team of people. They work together to sell something.
Some sell things you can hold, like shoes. Some sell things you use, like games or shows.
A shop that cuts hair is a company too. It sells help, not things.

steps.q: What does a company do?
options: Makes the rules for a town
steps.why: A company sells things, or help like haircuts, to people.

steps.text: Money in is all the money a company gets from selling things.
Money out is what it pays for. Workers, rent and supplies.
Money in take away money out is profit. If money out is bigger, that is a loss.

steps.q: Money in or money out?
steps.why: Selling brings money in. Paying for things sends money out.

steps.q: A cookie stand sells $20 of cookies. Its only cost is $5. What is the profit?
steps.why: $20 take away $5 is $15.

steps.text: A lemonade stand can grow into a lemonade shop.
To grow, it needs money for a bigger shop and more workers.
One way to get that money is to sell small pieces of the company. Those pieces are called shares.

steps.q: Why might a company sell shares?
steps.why: Selling shares brings in money the company can use to grow.

units.title: Shares and the market
units.blurb: Owning a tiny slice.
talk: If you owned a tiny slice of one company, which would you pick, and why?
Why might people want a company's shares more on some days than others?

steps.text: Think of a big company like a pizza cut into lots and lots of slices.
Each slice is called a share. If you own a share, you own a tiny piece of that company.
Owning a share does not mean you can take things from its stores. You own a tiny piece of the whole company.

steps.q: If you own a share of a company, you own…
steps.why: A share is a tiny slice of the company. Like one slice of a pizza.

steps.q: You own a share of a toy company. Can you take a toy from its store for free?
options: No, you own a tiny piece of the company
steps.why: A share is a tiny piece of the whole company, not the toys on the shelf.

steps.text: The stock market is a big place where people buy and sell shares.
Today it is mostly on computers. It opens in the morning and closes in the afternoon.
Most trades are between owners. When you buy a share, your money goes to the owner who sold it.
In New York, a bell rings to start the day and to end it!

steps.q: What do people trade on the stock market?
steps.why: The stock market is where shares are traded.

steps.q: Mia buys a share on the stock market. Who usually gets her money?
steps.why: Most trades are between owners. The seller gets the money.

lessons.title: Why do prices go up and down?

steps.text: Think of trading cards. When everyone wants one card, people will give more for it.
The price of a share is what someone will pay for it right now.
If buyers want shares more than sellers do, the price goes up. If sellers are in a hurry, it goes down.
Prices move every day. Small ups and downs are normal.

steps.q: Lots of people really want a share, and few want to sell. The price…
steps.why: When buyers want it more than sellers do, the price tends to go up.

steps.q: Is it normal for prices to move a little every day?
steps.why: Prices wiggle every day. That is normal.

steps.text: If you own a share, you are a part owner of the company.
Owners can vote on some big choices, like who helps lead the company. Most of the time, one share is one vote.
People often want a share more when they think the company will make more profit later.
A high price does not mean a better company. It depends on how many slices there are.

steps.q: Owning one share of a shoe company makes you…
options: A tiny part owner of it
steps.why: One share makes you a tiny part owner. Lots of other people own parts too.

steps.q: Shop A's share costs $100. Shop B's share costs $10. Which company is better?
options: You can't tell from the price
steps.why: Price alone doesn't tell you. It depends on how many slices there are.

steps.text: Each company on the market has a short nickname. It is called a ticker.
Apple is AAPL. Disney is DIS. Coca-Cola is KO.
Grown-ups use tickers to find a company fast.

steps.q: What is DIS?
steps.why: DIS is Disney's short nickname on the stock market.

units.title: Piggy Bank school
units.blurb: Practice with pretend coins, the smart way.
talk: Our pretend coins went down today. Is that a big move, or a normal wiggle?
How often should we check the Piggy Bank? Why not every minute?

steps.text: Your Piggy Bank has 1,000 pretend coins. You pick companies, and the coins follow their real prices.
This piggy bank is different from a real one. Its coins go up and down with prices.
It is all pretend. Nothing is bought for real, and no real money can be lost.

steps.q: Is Piggy Bank money real?
steps.why: It is pretend. It just follows real prices so you can learn.

steps.text: Put 200 coins in each of 5 companies. Now your 1,000 coins are spread out.
Grown-ups say: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. That means spread out!
Say one company loses half, and the others stay the same. You lose 100 coins. You still have 900.
Now say all 1,000 coins were in that one company. You would lose 500!

steps.q: Which piggy bank is hurt less by one bad company?
steps.why: When coins are spread out, one bad company only hurts a small part.

steps.q: Spread out or all in one?

items.text: All coins on one tip from a video

steps.why: Spreading out means one bad company hurts less.

steps.text: Your Piggy Bank line will zig and zag. That is normal!
A down day is like a rainy day. It does not mean you did something wrong.
When it drops, take a breath. Ask: Is this a big move, or a normal wiggle?

steps.q: Your piggy bank went down a little today. What does it mean?
steps.why: Small ups and downs happen every day. They are normal.

steps.text: Prices change every minute. Peeking every minute can make you feel worried.
Up close, tiny wiggles look huge. From far away, they look small.
Try checking once a day or once a week. Then you see the bigger picture.

steps.q: How often is a good time to check your piggy bank?
steps.why: Checking now and then keeps the wiggles small and your mind calm.

steps.text: Over one day, prices bounce up and down a lot.
Zoom out to many years. In the past, the US market went up in more years than it went down.
That is history, not a promise. But it is why grown-ups often invest for a long time.

steps.q: Why do many grown-ups invest for many years?
options: Time can smooth out the bumps
steps.why: Over many years, the bumps matter less. It is still not a promise.

units.title: Saving and investing
units.blurb: Keep it safe, or help it grow.
talk: If you had $10, would you save it or invest it? What is it for, and when?
In the Moon Garden, what happens to points the longer they grow?

steps.text: Saving is keeping your money safe, like in a jar at home. The number stays the same.
Investing is using money to buy things like shares. It can grow, but it can also shrink.
Grown-ups often do both. They save money they need soon. They invest money they will not need for a long time.

steps.q: Money in a jar at home…
steps.why: Jar money stays the same number. It does not grow by itself.

steps.q: Investing can make money…
steps.why: Investing can go up or down. That is the risk.

steps.text: A bank keeps your money safe. Savings accounts often pay you a little to keep it there.
That little extra is called interest. Put in $100, and a year later you may have $102.
Prices of things often go up over time. So the same $10 may buy a bit less later.
Interest is slow, but bank savings are very safe.

steps.q: Interest is…
options: A little extra the bank pays you
The money you first put in
Money that buys more every year
steps.why: It is the small extra the bank adds to your money.

steps.text: Risk means things might not go the way you hope.
A savings jar has low risk. It will not grow much, but it will not shrink.
Investing has more risk. It can grow more, but some years it goes down.

steps.q: Low risk or high risk?

items.text: Coins in a jar at home
All your money in one new company
A stock a video says will "go to the moon"

steps.why: Jars and banks grow slowly or not at all, but rarely shrink. One hot stock can swing a lot.

steps.text: Roll a snowball and it picks up more snow. It gets bigger as it rolls.
Money can do that too. Say $100 grows to $110. Next year, all $110 can grow.
Starting early gives the snowball more time to roll. Some years it can shrink, too.

steps.q: Why does starting early help?
options: More time for money to grow
steps.why: More years means more time for growth to pile up.

steps.text: 10% a year means $10 more for every $100. Like your Moon Garden, real money can grow.
$100 grows 10% a year. Growth on growth vs the same $10 each year. Tap to grow.
steps.label: Growth on growth

steps.text: Growth on growth is called compound growth. It is slow at first, then speeds up. Pretend numbers, no promises.

steps.q: $100 grows 10% a year, growth on growth. After 2 years it is…

steps.text: Grown-ups use a quick trick called the Rule of 72. Divide 72 by the yearly growth.
Money grows 10% a year. About how long until it doubles?
Check the trick: $100 at 10% a year. Close to $200 at year 7, past it in year 8. A near guess!
steps.label: 10% a year

steps.q: Money grows 8% a year. About how long to double?
steps.why: 72 ÷ 8 = 9. So about 9 years. It is a rough guess, not a promise.

steps.text: Need the money soon? Save it. Then it will be there when you need it.
Is it for something many years away? Investing gives it time to grow, and time to bounce back. No promises.

steps.q: Save it or invest it?

items.text: A gift for a friend this month
Money for when you are a grown-up

steps.why: Soon means save. A long time away means it could be invested.

units.title: Prices over time
units.blurb: Why things cost more later, and what that means.
talk: Ask an older relative or neighbor what a movie ticket or a candy bar cost when they were your age.
Pick something we buy often. Write down its price, and check it again in six months.
Why might money in a jar buy less in a few years, even though it is still the same number?

steps.text: When your grandparents were kids, a candy bar cost much less than it does now.
When most prices go up over time, it is called inflation.
Say a cart of food costs $100. Prices go up 3% a year. 3% means $3 more for every $100.
Tap to see the cart's price go up, year after year.
steps.label: Cart of food

steps.q: Inflation means…
options: Most prices go up over time
steps.why: Inflation is when most prices go up over time.

steps.text: Jar money stays the same number. But if prices go up, it buys a bit less.
Say prices go up. A toy costs $10 today, and $11 next year.

steps.q: Prices go up, but your jar money stays the same. What happens?
steps.why: The number stays the same, but each thing costs more. So it buys less.

steps.text: Say a bank pays 1% a year. But prices go up 3% a year.
Watch a $100 cart of food and $100 of bank savings over 5 years.
steps.label: Cart of food

steps.text: Bank savings are safe for money you need soon. Some grown-ups invest for the long run. It can grow or shrink.

steps.q: Savings grow 1% a year. Prices grow 3%. Your savings buy…
steps.why: Prices grow faster than the savings, so the savings buy a bit less.

units.title: Borrowing and interest
units.blurb: Borrow, pay back, and the price of borrowing.
talk: Have you ever lent something to a friend? What made you trust them to give it back?
If you borrowed $10 and paid back $11, what is the extra $1 for?
Why do you think lenders want to know if someone paid back on time before?

steps.text: When you save in a bank, the bank often pays you a little interest.
When you borrow, it flips around. You pay interest to the lender.
You borrow $100. The interest is $10 for one year.

steps.q: Why do borrowers pay back more than they borrowed?
steps.why: Interest is what the borrower pays for using the lender's money.

steps.text: Banks lend money because borrowers pay them interest. Lending earns them money.
Lenders like to lend to people who pay back on time.

steps.q: Who would you rather lend your bike to?
options: A friend who always gives things back
A friend who lost your last toy
steps.why: You trust people who gave things back before. Lenders think the same way.

steps.q: How does a bank earn money from lending?
steps.why: Borrowers pay back more than they borrowed. The extra is interest.

steps.text: A credit card is a loan you can use at stores.
Each month a bill comes. Pay all of it by the due date, and you usually pay no interest.
Pay only part, and interest is added to the rest. Card interest is often high.

steps.q: When does a credit card usually cost no interest?
options: When you pay the whole bill on time
steps.why: Paying the whole bill by the due date usually means no interest.

steps.text: Interest can make savings grow like a snowball. What you owe can grow the same way.
Say Max owes $100 and pays nothing back. The interest is 20% a year. Tap to see what he owes.
steps.label: What Max owes

steps.text: Paying back on time, and in full, keeps what you owe small. Then interest has little to grow on.

steps.q: Max owes $100 at 20% a year and pays nothing. After 2 years he owes…

units.title: Dividends
units.blurb: When your slice pays you.
talk: Why might a company keep all its profit instead of paying a dividend?
Would you spend a dividend or use it to buy more shares? Why?

steps.text: Some companies give part of their profit to their owners. That is a dividend.
If you own a share, you might get a little money every few months.
Many big, older companies pay them. Some do not. A company can cut or stop its dividend.

steps.q: A dividend is…
options: Profit a company gives its owners
Money you pay to buy a share
A fee the company charges you
steps.why: It is a bit of the profit. The owners get it.

steps.text: Some companies keep all their profit to grow faster.
They build new things, hire workers and open new stores.
Owners hope the company grows. Then their shares may be worth more later. That is a hope, not a promise.

steps.q: Why might a company skip dividends?
options: To use the money to grow
steps.why: Some companies use all their profit to grow.

steps.text: When you get a dividend, you can spend it. Or you can use it to buy more shares.
Buying more shares is like adding snow to your snowball.
Both are okay choices. Buying more shares can add up over many years.

steps.q: Using dividends to buy more shares is like…
steps.why: More shares can pay you more. So the snowball grows.

steps.text: Each dividend has a cut-off day. You must own the share before that day to get the payout.
On that day, the share price often drops by about the size of the payout.
The money did not vanish. It moved from the company to its owners.

steps.q: A $50 share pays a $1 dividend. On the cut-off day, the price might be about…
steps.why: The price often drops by about the payout. $50 take away $1 is about $49.

steps.text: To compare dividends, grown-ups ask: how much is paid for each $100 of shares?
A $50 share pays $2 a year.
A company can cut its dividend. A big payout is not a promise.

steps.q: A $25 share pays $1 a year. For each $100, it pays…
steps.why: $100 buys 4 shares. 4 × $1 = $4 for each $100, or 4%.

units.title: Baskets of companies
units.blurb: Funds, index funds, fees and spreading out.
talk: If you made a basket with one share of every company you know, which companies would be in it?
Do toy companies all have good and bad years at the same time? Why might they?
Why might a fund with a lower fee leave more money for its owners?

steps.text: Companies in the same group often move together. Like toy makers, or food makers.
So three toy companies are not very spread out. One bad toy year can hurt them all.
Spreading across groups helps more. Food, games and shoes don't always move together.

steps.q: Which is more spread out?
steps.why: Different groups rarely all have a bad year at once. But in a big market drop, most fall together.

steps.text: A fund is like a basket that holds shares of many companies.
One fund share is a tiny slice of the basket, so you own a bit of every company in it.
If one company has a bad year, it is only a small part of the basket. A fund can still go down.

steps.q: One share of a fund gives you…
options: A tiny bit of many companies
A promise it only goes up
steps.why: A fund holds many companies, so one share is a tiny bit of each one.

steps.text: A fee is what you pay for a service. Funds take a small fee every year.
Two funds hold the same companies, which grow 7% a year. Pretend: one fee is tiny, one is 1% a year.
steps.label: Tiny fee

steps.text: A small fee each year adds up over many years. Grown-ups check fees before they pick a fund.

steps.q: Two funds hold the same companies. Which usually leaves you more?
options: The one with the lower fee
The one with the higher fee
steps.why: Same companies, so the lower fee usually leaves more for the owners.

steps.text: An index is a list of companies. One famous list has about 500 big US companies.
An index fund buys the companies on its list. Nobody picks winners. If they fall, the fund falls too.
Since nobody picks, index funds are often cheap to run. Their fees are often low.

steps.q: What does an index fund do?
options: Buys the companies on a list
steps.why: It buys every company on its list, instead of trying to pick winners.

units.title: Money-smart
units.blurb: Spread out, be patient, check facts.
talk: How could we check if a video about a stock is true? Who made it, and why?
What is a red flag that something is too good to be true?

lessons.title: Don't put all your eggs in one basket

steps.text: Imagine you carry all your eggs in one basket. If you trip, they all break!
If you split them into many baskets, one trip only breaks a few.
Money works the same way. A little of many companies is usually safer than a lot of one.
Spreading out helps when one company has trouble. If the whole market drops, most baskets drop together.

steps.q: Why split your eggs into many baskets?
options: So one trip doesn't break them all
So you can carry more eggs
steps.why: If one basket falls, the others are still safe.

steps.q: Which is usually safer?
options: All your money in one company
steps.why: Spreading out means one bad company hurts less.

steps.text: The moon takes about two weeks to go from new moon to full moon. It does not rush.
Some companies grow over many years. Some days their price goes down. Some days it goes up.
People who invest for a long time often do better than people who buy and sell every day.

steps.q: Good investing is usually…
steps.why: In the past, waiting a long time has often worked better than rushing.

steps.q: A price goes down for one day. Is that a reason to worry a lot?
steps.why: Prices go up and down. One bad day is normal.

steps.text: Sometimes a video says a stock will "go to the moon". That is called hype.
Hype is exciting. But the person in the video might want something from you, or might just be wrong.
Facts are things you can check, like how much profit a company made.
Before you believe a video, ask: What are the facts? Who is telling me this? Why?

steps.q: A video says "this stock will go to the moon!" That is…
steps.why: It's an exciting guess, not a fact you can check.

steps.q: What should you do before believing a video?
options: Check the facts with a grown-up
steps.why: Always check the facts, and ask a grown-up.

steps.text: If someone promises lots of money, fast and for sure, that is a red flag.
Real investing has ups and downs. Nobody can promise it only goes up.
If it feels too good to be true, stop and ask a grown-up.

steps.q: Someone says "Double your money by Friday, for sure!" What do you do?
steps.why: Big promises that are "for sure" are a red flag. Ask a grown-up.

steps.text: Your Piggy Bank line shows what prices did before. It is a clue.
A clue is not a promise. News and surprises can change the price fast.
People who know a lot still guess wrong. That is normal.

steps.q: A price went up three days in a row. What does that tell you?
options: It is a clue, not a promise
steps.why: Three days up is only a clue. Nobody knows for sure what comes next.

steps.q: Who knows for sure what a price will do next?
steps.why: Nobody can know for sure. Not even experts.

units.title: Report cards
units.blurb: Guesses, beats, misses and what comes next.
talk: Pick a company we know and look at when its next report card is. What do you guess?
Why do you think a price went down even though the company beat the guess?

steps.text: You get a report card from school. Companies get one too!
Big US companies tell everyone how they did four times a year. Grown-ups call this an earnings report.
It says how much money came in, and how much profit the company made.
Moon Club shows how long until each report card. We draw that wait as a moon.

steps.q: How many times a year does a big US company share its report card?
steps.why: Big US companies report four times a year, about once every three months.

steps.q: What do grown-ups call a company's report card?
steps.why: It is called an earnings report.

steps.text: Companies say ahead of time which day their report card comes out. Moon Club's moon counts down to it.
Some share it before the market opens. Some share it after it closes.
Either way, the big price move usually shows up the next time the market is open.
Some grown-ups trade after hours, so the price can start moving that night.

steps.q: A company reports after the market closes on Tuesday. When does the big move usually show?
steps.why: After the close, most people can trade again the next morning, Wednesday.

steps.text: Before a report card, experts guess the profit for each share. Their guess is called an estimate.
Lots of experts guess. Grown-ups mix all the guesses into one number, the average. That is the number to beat.
Then everyone waits to see what really happened.

steps.q: What are the experts guessing?
options: The company's profit for each share
steps.why: They guess the profit, so we can see if the company beats it.

steps.q: Three experts guess $1, $2 and $3. Their average is $2. What is the number to beat?
steps.why: $1 + $2 + $3 is $6. Split by 3, that is $2, the number to beat.

steps.text: It is like guessing how many jellybeans are in a jar. Then you count them!
If the company makes more than the guess, it beat. If it makes less, it missed.

steps.q: Grown-ups guessed $2. The company made $3. Did it beat or miss?
steps.why: $3 is more than the $2 guess, so it beat.

steps.q: Grown-ups guessed $2. The company made $1. Did it beat or miss?
steps.why: $1 is less than the $2 guess, so it missed.

lessons.title: Why prices jump on report day

steps.text: On report card day, prices can jump up or fall down fast.
That is because people learn lots of new facts all at once.
They also hear what the company thinks comes next.

steps.q: Why can a price jump on report card day?
options: People learn new facts all at once
The market closes early that day
steps.why: New facts arrive all at once, so people change their minds fast.

steps.text: A company is cut into many shares. Its profit can be split the same way.
A lemonade company makes $1,000 profit. It has 100 shares.
That is the number experts guess before report day: the profit for each share.

steps.q: Profit is $600. There are 200 shares. Profit for each share?
steps.why: $600 split into 200 shares is $3 for each share.

steps.text: A report card shows two big numbers. Sales are the money customers paid for what the company sold.
Profit is what is left after paying all the costs.
Last year: sales $50, costs $30.
lines: Profit now: $15. Sold more, kept less!

steps.text: A company can sell more and still make less profit, if its costs grew even more.

steps.q: Sales went up $10. Costs went up $15. Profit…
steps.why: Costs grew $5 more than sales, so profit went down $5.

lessons.title: Why a beat can still drop

steps.text: Imagine you hope for a big cake on your birthday. You get a cupcake. Yum, but you hoped for more!
Prices work like that. Before report day, people already hope for things. Those hopes are in the price.
So a company can beat the guess and its price can still drop. People hoped for even more.
It works the other way too. A miss can still go up if people feared even worse.

steps.q: A company beat the guess, but its price went down. Why might that be?
options: A beat always makes prices drop
steps.why: People hoped for even more, so a small beat let them down.

steps.q: Does a beat always make the price go up?
steps.why: No. What people hoped for matters too.

steps.text: On report day, many companies also say what they think will happen next. That is called guidance.
If a company says next time looks great, people may cheer. If it says it looks slow, people may worry.
Guidance is the company's own guess. It can be wrong too.

steps.q: A company beat this time, but says next time looks slow. What might happen to the price?
steps.why: People care about what comes next, not just today. A slow forecast can make the price drop.

steps.q: Guidance is…
options: What a company thinks will happen next
A promise that can't be wrong
steps.why: Guidance is the company's own guess about what comes next.

steps.text: A beat can be tiny or big. How big the surprise is matters too.
Experts guessed $2.00 for each share. The company made $2.50.
lines: 50¢ is one fourth of $2, or 25% more

steps.text: Even a big beat can drop, if the company says next time looks slow.

steps.q: Guess: $1.00 a share. Result: $1.01. How big is the surprise?
steps.why: One cent more on a $1 guess is a very small beat.

units.title: Why did it move?
units.blurb: Clues for why a price went up or down.
talk: When a price jumps, what clues could we check before we guess why?
Is "we're not sure" an okay answer? When have you said it?

steps.text: Every price wiggles a little every day, even with no news.
Each company has its own normal wiggle size. Some wiggle a lot. Some wiggle a little.
A big move is a clue that something happened. A small move is often just a wiggle.

steps.q: A price moved just a tiny bit today. What is it most likely?
steps.why: Small moves happen every day. They are usually just wiggles.

steps.text: Some days, almost every price goes up. Some days, almost every price goes down.
That is the whole market moving, like weather over a whole town.
So if your company dropped, check: Did the whole market drop too?

steps.q: Almost every company went down today. Yours did too. What is a good clue?
steps.why: When almost everything drops, the whole market is a big clue.

steps.text: Companies that do the same kind of work are a group. Like all the game makers.
News about one game maker can move the whole group, up or down together.
Grown-ups call a group like this a sector.

steps.q: Lots of game makers went up today. What might be a clue?
options: News about games moved the group
steps.why: Groups often move together, so news about the group is a clue.

steps.text: Sometimes a price moves and nobody can say why for sure.
Good detectives say "we're not sure yet" instead of making up a story.
We look at clues: report cards, the whole market, the group and the size of the move.

steps.q: A price moved and there are no clues. What is the honest answer?
options: It will keep going that way
steps.why: Honest detectives say when they don't know. Making up a reason isn't fair.

units.title: Candles
units.blurb: A whole day of a price in one tiny picture.
talk: Draw a candle for a day when the price started at $10, went up to $12 and ended at $11.

steps.text: A candle is a tiny picture of one day of a price.
The fat part is the body. It shows where the price started and where it ended.
Green means the price ended higher than it started. Red means it ended lower. In some countries, red means up!
A chart shows what already happened. It is a clue, not a promise.

steps.q: A candle is green. What happened that day?
options: It ended higher than it started
It ended lower than it started
steps.why: Green means it ended higher than it started.

steps.text: The thin lines on the top and bottom are called wicks.
The top of the wick is the highest price that day. The bottom is the lowest.
A long wick means the price went far, then came back.

steps.q: What does the top of the wick show?
steps.why: The top of the wick is the highest the price got that day.

steps.q: Green or red candle?
steps.why: Ended higher is green. Ended lower is red.

steps.text: Some days, buyers and sellers pull hard both ways, like a game of tug-of-war.
The price goes way up and way down, but ends near where it started.
That candle has a tiny body and long wicks on top and bottom.

steps.q: A candle has a tiny body and long wicks. What kind of day was it?
steps.why: Long wicks and a tiny body mean the price swung both ways.

units.title: Trends
units.blurb: Up, down or sideways over many days.
talk: Look at a chart together. Is the trend up, down or sideways? What happens if we zoom out?

steps.text: A trend is the way a price has been going over many days.
If the price keeps climbing over many days, the trend is up. Each high and each low is a bit higher.
If the price keeps sliding over many days, the trend is down. Each high and each low is a bit lower.
Prices wiggle every day. Look at the big picture, not one day.

steps.q: A price wiggles but keeps climbing for a month. The trend is…
steps.why: It keeps climbing, so the trend is up, even with wiggles.

steps.text: Sometimes a price goes up, then down, then up again, but stays in the same small range.
That is a sideways trend. It is like walking on flat ground.

steps.q: A price stays between $9 and $11 for a whole month. The trend is…
steps.why: It stayed in a small, flat range, so it went sideways.

steps.text: A trend shows what already happened. It does not promise what comes next.

steps.q: Does an up trend promise the price will keep going up?
steps.why: A trend can change any day. It is a clue, not a promise.

steps.text: One day can look scary. Many days can tell a calmer story.
Zoom out to see more days. The trend is easier to spot.
People who invest for years look at years, not days.

steps.q: One small red day in a month of green days. What is the trend?
steps.why: One small red day does not change a month of going up.

units.title: Floors and ceilings
units.blurb: Spots a price keeps bouncing off.
talk: Why do you think chart shapes look so clear only after they happen?

steps.text: Sometimes a price keeps falling to the same low spot, then bounces. That spot is the floor.
Sometimes a price keeps stopping at the same high spot. That spot is the ceiling.
Grown-ups call the floor support. They call the ceiling resistance.
Floors and ceilings can break. They show where the price turned before, not where it must turn.

steps.q: A price keeps bouncing up from $20. What is $20?
steps.why: A spot it keeps bouncing up from is the floor.

steps.text: When a price pushes up through its ceiling, that is a breakout.
When a price falls through its floor, that is a breakdown.
Lots of breakouts fail. The price can fall right back. That is normal!

steps.q: The ceiling was $50. Now the price is $55. What happened?
steps.why: It pushed up through the ceiling. That is a breakout.

steps.q: After a breakout, the price…
options: Might keep going, or fall back
steps.why: A breakout is a clue, not a promise. Many fall back.

steps.text: After a price moves, its chart shape can look so clear. Of course it went up!
But on that day, nobody knew which way it would go. Lots of shapes just fizzle out.
That is why shapes are clues. Looking back is easy. Looking ahead is hard.

steps.q: A chart shape looks obvious after the price moved. Did people know on that day?
options: No, it only looks clear now
Yes, the shape was a promise
steps.why: Looking back is easy. On the day, nobody knew for sure.

units.title: Busy days and smooth lines
units.blurb: Volume, averages and report-day jumps.
talk: Why might more people trade a company's shares on its report card day?

steps.text: Volume means how many shares people traded in a day.
A busy day has lots of trading. A quiet day has less.
Report card days are often busy. Lots of people react to the news.

steps.q: What does volume tell you?
steps.why: Volume counts how many shares changed hands.

steps.text: Prices zig and zag. That can make the trend hard to see.
Prices of $4, $6 and $5 add up to $15. Split by 3, the average is $5.
Find that average again every day, and you get a smooth line. It helps you see the trend.
The smooth line only looks back. It does not know what comes next.

steps.q: Why do people use a moving average?
options: To see the trend more easily
To make the price go up
steps.why: The smooth line hides the wiggles, so the trend is easier to see.

steps.text: On report card day, a price can jump up or drop down fast.
On a chart, report day often has a tall candle and big volume.
A beat can still drop, and a miss can still rise. Hopes matter.

steps.q: A company beat the guess. Will the price always go up?
steps.why: Not always. People may have wanted even more.

company.means: A team of people who sell something to make money.
company.example: A bike shop is a company. It sells bikes.

profit.means: The money left after a company pays its bills.
profit.example: You sell lemonade for $10. The lemons cost $4. You keep $6.

share.means: A tiny slice of a company that someone can own.
share.example: Cut a giant pizza into a million slices. One slice is one share.

stock.means: A big market where people buy and sell shares.
stock.example: It is like a giant trading-card swap, but for slices of companies.

price.means: What someone will pay for one share right now.
price.example: When lots of kids want a card, it costs more.

report.means: A company tells how much money it made. Big US companies do it 4 times a year.
report.example: Lots of them come out in spring, summer, fall and winter.

guess.means: Before the report card, experts guess the profit for each share. It is also called an estimate.
guess.example: They guess $2. That is the number to beat.

beat.means: The company made more than the grown-ups guessed.
beat.example: They guessed $2. It made $3. It beat!

miss.means: The company made less than the grown-ups guessed.
miss.example: They guessed $2. It made $1. It missed.

mood.means: How people feel about buying shares today: hopeful or worried.
mood.example: Sun means hope. A storm means worry.

saving.means: Keeping money safe so you can use it later.
saving.example: You put $10 in a jar. Next month, it is still $10.

investing.means: Using money to buy things like shares, hoping they grow.
investing.example: It can grow more than a jar, but it can shrink too.

interest.means: A little extra money the bank pays you for keeping your money there.
interest.example: Keep $10 in the bank for a year. Get 20 cents extra.

dividend.means: A little of a company's profit, shared with each owner.
dividend.example: Own one share. The company pays you $1 of its profit.

candle.means: A tiny picture of one day of a price.
candle.example: A green candle means the price ended higher that day.

wick.means: The thin line on a candle. It shows the highest and lowest price that day.
wick.example: A long wick means the price went far, then came back.

trend.means: The way a price has been going over many days: up, down or sideways.
trend.example: Each high and each low is higher than the last one, so the trend is up.

support.means: A low spot a price has bounced up from before.
support.example: The price fell to $20 three times and bounced each time. Floors can still break.

resistance.means: A high spot a price has stopped at before.
resistance.example: The price hit $50 twice and turned back down.

breakout.means: When a price pushes up through its ceiling.
breakout.example: The ceiling was $50. Now it is $55. Lots of breakouts fail, too.

pattern.means: A shape on a chart. It is a clue, not a promise.
pattern.example: Two hills in a row is a pattern. The next day can still surprise you.

volume.means: How many shares people traded in a day.
volume.example: Report card days often have big volume.

average.means: A smooth line made from the average of the last few prices.
average.example: It hides the wiggles, so the trend is easier to see. It only looks back.

tradeoff.means: What you give up when you pick one thing over another.
tradeoff.example: You buy the kite, so you can't buy the book. The book is the trade-off.

expectations.means: What people already think will happen. Prices include these hopes.
expectations.example: A company can beat the guess and still drop if people hoped for more.

guidance.means: What a company says it thinks will happen next.
guidance.example: "Next time looks slow" is guidance. It can be wrong too.

sector.means: Companies that do the same kind of work.
sector.example: All the game makers are one group. They often move together.

diversify.means: Owning a little of many things instead of a lot of one.
diversify.example: 200 pretend coins in 5 companies is spread out.

fund.means: A basket that holds a little of many companies at once.
fund.example: Some shares are pieces of a fund. One fund can hold hundreds of companies.

wiggle.means: The small ups and downs a price makes every day, even with no news.
wiggle.example: Up a little, down a little. That is a wiggle.

wage.means: Pay for each hour of work.
wage.example: Leo's wage is $10 an hour. Three hours pay $30.

tax.means: Money people pay the government for things we share.
tax.example: Taxes help pay for schools, roads and fire trucks.

entrepreneur.means: A person who starts a business and takes a risk.
entrepreneur.example: A kid who starts a lemonade stand is an entrepreneur.

goal.example: Save $10 a week for 6 weeks to buy a $60 bike.

emergency.example: When the bike tire popped, the rainy day fund paid for it.

loan.means: Money you borrow and must pay back.
loan.example: Borrow $100, and pay back $110 with interest.

credit.means: A card that lets you borrow money you must pay back.
credit.example: Pay the whole bill on time, and there is usually no interest.

inflation.means: When most prices go up over time.
inflation.example: If most prices go up 3%, a $100 cart of food costs about $103 next year.

index.means: A fund that buys all the companies on one list.
index.example: One list has about 500 big US companies in it.

fee.means: Money you pay for a service.
fee.example: A fund takes a small fee every year.

insurance.means: Many people pay a little, so one with bad luck gets help.
insurance.example: Car insurance helps pay to fix a dented car.

premium.means: The small amount each person pays for insurance.
premium.example: Lots of people pay a premium each month.

debit.means: A card that pays with money from your own bank account.
debit.example: Pay $5 with a debit card, and $5 leaves your account.

salary.means: The same pay each year, split into paychecks.
salary.example: A teacher gets a salary, paid every two weeks.

tip.means: Extra money a customer gives for good help.
tip.example: Mom left a $2 tip for the server.

scam.means: A trick to take your money or your account.
scam.example: "Free gems for your password" is a scam.

sales.means: All the money a company gets from selling.
sales.example: Sales are money in. Profit is what is left after costs.

words.means: A tiny piece of a company that you can own.
words.example: If a company were a pizza, one share would be one small slice.

words.means: The money a company has left after it pays all its bills.
words.example: You sell lemonade for $10. The lemons cost $4. Your profit is $6.

words.means: A company's profit. The earnings report is its report card.
words.example: A big US company reports its earnings four times a year.

words.means: When a company does better than grown-ups guessed.
words.example: Grown-ups guessed $1. It made $2. It beat!

words.means: When a company does worse than grown-ups guessed.
words.example: Grown-ups guessed $2. It made $1. It missed.

words.means: The place where people buy and sell shares.
words.example: It's like a giant trading card swap, but for companies.

words.means: What someone will pay for one share right now.
words.example: If many people want a share, its price often goes up.

words.means: Using money now so it might grow later.

words.means: Keeping money safe so you can use it later.

tips.report-card: Big US companies share how they did four times a year. That is their report card.
tips.guess: Before report day, experts guess the profit for each share. Their average is the number to beat.
tips.beat: Made more than the guess? It beat. Made less? It missed.
tips.expectations: A beat can still make the price drop if people hoped for even more.
tips.guidance: Listen for what comes next. A company's guess about next time can move the price.
tips.after: Report day can be bumpy. New facts arrive all at once.
tips.calendar: Report day is set ahead of time. After the close, the big move usually shows up the next morning.
tips.per-share: Experts guess the profit for each share. That is the company's profit split across all its shares.
tips.sales-profit: Sales are money from customers. Profit is what's left after costs. More sales can still mean less profit.
tips.surprise: A beat can be tiny or big. A tiny beat may not mean much, and other news can still move the price a lot.

reveal.beatUp: It beat the guess, and the price went up. People may have liked the news.
reveal.beatDown: It beat the guess, but the price went down. People may have hoped for even more, or worried about what comes next.
reveal.missDown: It missed the guess, and the price went down. People may have been let down.
reveal.missUp: It missed the guess, but the price went up. Maybe people feared worse, or liked what it said about next time.
reveal.unknown: We don't know the price move yet. Check back soon!
reveal.inLine: It matched the guess exactly. Then hopes and what comes next matter most.
reveal.tryAgain: Good thinking! Even experts guess wrong a lot. That is how we learn.

tips.oneBasket: All your coins are in one basket. If that company has a bad day, all your pretend coins feel it.
tips.fewBaskets: {n} baskets! If one company has a bad day, the others can help balance it out.
tips.manyBaskets: {n} baskets: nicely spread out! One bad company won't spoil the whole bunch.
tips.newBank: Your Piggy Bank is brand new. Prices need time. Come back in a few days!
tips.longTime: Your Piggy Bank is {days} days old. Look at the whole line, not just today.
tips.bigDrop: Your pretend coins are down {pct}% since you started. Big drops happen to everyone. It is not your fault.
tips.bigRise: Your pretend coins are up {pct}% since you started. Prices can fall again too. Spreading out is still a good habit.
tips.peekMany: You've looked {n} times today. Curious is great! Prices wiggle all day, so once a day is plenty.
tips.oneGroup: Your {n} companies are all in the same group. Groups often move together, so they may all have a bad day at once.
